name: Adam Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing gets your name on it. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm in my third year as an apprentice on a distribution crew for the city's power company, the public one, so it's the poles and wires on regular streets, not the big towers. We meet at the yard on Harbour Road at seven, the foreman hands out the jobs, and most days I'm the one on the ground sending up tools and rigging while the journeymen work up top. A journeyman is a fully qualified lineworker, which I'm not yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that you can see what you did. You swap a cracked crossarm, the lights on that block stay on, done. What wears me out is storm calls, sixteen hours in the rain, and being the slowest guy on the crew. I came into this late, at twenty-four, after four years in a warehouse, so I'm still catching up on stuff the younger apprentices picked up faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the yard we already get emails about AI this and AI that, and none of it has climbed a pole yet. Online I'd probably share something from the union page saying the hype was about selling stock, not helping workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I get to finish my apprenticeship in peace, which is all I want. I'm not great with new tech and I don't use any of those AI apps, so a world where they stay small suits me fine. Nobody's going to ask a chatbot to fix a transformer at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going exactly as I am. Finish my last two years, sit my journeyman test, keep paying into the savings account, which is about three months of rent and bills right now. Maybe go to a couple more union meetings, but that's just because I've been meaning to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm being honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the emails at the yard are already about AI. What do those emails actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that the dispatch office is testing some program to plan routes and schedules. My foreman, Rob, reads them out loud in a silly voice. He's been doing this thirty years and he says every few years there's a new thing that's going to change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you, even a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that the office people get faster and we don't get anything out of it. If a program saves them hours, I'd want some of that to come back to the crews as better staffing. But in this picture I don't think it changes much for me.

S0.say: I'd tell people I knew the AI talk was hype, mostly there to sell shares. At the yard we'd laugh about it, because none of it has climbed a pole yet.
S0.think: Privately I'm relieved, because it means I can finish my apprenticeship without anything new to learn. I don't use AI tools and a world where they stay small suits me.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal, finishes the last two years of his apprenticeship and sits his journeyman test. Keeps adding to his savings, which cover about three months of costs.
S0.quote: Nobody's going to ask a chatbot to fix a transformer at two in the morning.
S0.fieldNote: Adam came into the trade late and still feels behind, which makes him want the ground to stay still. He frames even the mild picture through the union lens: who keeps the time saved. No sign of fear here, just quiet satisfaction that the hype didn't land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: if the company saves money with this stuff, the workers should share in it. I'd be the guy in the break room saying watch the staffing numbers, not the press releases. Online I'd probably just repost things, I'm not much of a writer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the poles still need people, so I'm not that scared for the climbing part. What scares me is the office using AI to squeeze us, like cutting a five-man crew to four because a program says it's enough. If they cut a guy, it's the slow apprentice they cut, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting instead of every other one, and I'd sign whatever petition they put out about crew sizes. I'd keep saving, maybe push it from three months to five by skipping the new truck I wanted. I wouldn't learn the AI stuff unless they forced me, and if they did I'd do the minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not like the floor's gone, more like someone's measuring it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip the new truck. Tell me about that truck.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a used pickup I've been eyeing at a lot on the ring road, nothing fancy. Lena, my partner, says I should just get it because my old one keeps failing inspection. But if things are shifting, I'd rather fix the old one again and keep the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatchers, maybe, more than us. There's a woman named Priya who's been doing it for years, and if a program can plan the day, I don't know what happens to her. And the other apprentices who are behind like me.

S1.say: I'd repeat the union line that if the company saves money with AI, workers should get a share. I'd tell people at work to watch crew sizes, not the press releases.
S1.think: I think the climbing work stays human, but I'm scared the office will use AI to cut crew numbers. If they cut someone, it'll be the slowest apprentice, and that's me.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting and signs petitions on crew sizes. Puts off buying a used truck to push his savings from about three to five months.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like someone is measuring the ground under him.
S1.quote: If they cut a guy, it's the slow apprentice they cut, and that's me.
S1.fieldNote: His worry isn't robots but management using software as an excuse to trim crews. He knows exactly where he sits in the pecking order and says so plainly. He'd lean on the union rather than change himself, and he admits he'd do the bare minimum of any AI training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, for me anyway. I'd say this is exactly why we need laws, that you can't let a few tech companies flip the whole country's work over in two years. At the yard I'd be telling everyone to get to the union hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is basically tomorrow for me. I won't even have my journeyman card by then, so I'd be a half-trained apprentice in a trade that's getting robots. I spent four years in a warehouse to get out of a job a machine could do. Now I'd be right back there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, today, and try to get the savings past five months. I'd go to the union and push hard for some kind of rule that robots on the lines need a human crew, and I'd vote for whoever promises that. I would not go learn how to run the robots, I know myself, I'd be bad at it and they'd pick someone younger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like getting the wind knocked out of you. I'd be up at night doing math on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would you say to Lena that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably tell her it's going to be okay, which is a lie. Her job's in a hospital, so maybe she's safer, or maybe not, I really don't know. I'd say we might have to live on her pay for a while and I'd hate saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn to run the robots. Even if that's where the jobs are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know how that sounds. I took three tries to pass the rigging part of my course, and I'm supposed to beat the kids who grew up on tablets at running a robot? I'd rather spend the energy fighting for rules that keep people on the job.

S2.say: We need laws, because you can't let a few tech companies flip everyone's work over in two years. Everyone at the yard should get down to the union hall.
S2.think: Two years means I'd still be a half-trained apprentice when the robots arrive. I left a warehouse job to get away from machines and I'd be right back in the same spot.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent and food straight away and tries to lift savings past five months. Pushes the union for rules requiring human crews with robots and votes for candidates who back that.
S2.feel: Winded and sleepless, doing money sums at the kitchen table.
S2.quote: I spent four years in a warehouse to get out of a job a machine could do. Now I'd be right back there.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version hits him hard because of timing: he'd never finish his apprenticeship. He openly refuses to retrain, and the reason is self-doubt more than stubbornness. All his hope goes into the union and the law, and he admits he'd lie to his partner to keep her calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but with more time to organise. I'd say five years is enough time for the union and the government to set rules, so let's not waste it. I'd probably even speak at a meeting, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd get my card, at least. I'd be a qualified lineworker for two or three years before it lands. That counts for something, but I'd still be the junior guy with the least years when they start picking who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish my apprenticeship fast and do every overtime shift I can get to build the savings, maybe to six months. I'd get onto the union's safety committee, because I think robots near live lines is where they'll have to listen to us. I'd keep putting money aside instead of the truck, again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less of a punch than the two-year one, but a long squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd speak at a meeting. What would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like, we're the ones who know what a live line does when it goes wrong, so nobody puts a robot on our poles without us signing off. I'd want them to remember the robot doesn't get electrocuted, but the guy standing next to it does. That's the kind of thing that gets the old guys nodding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd do for yourself, not just the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd maybe look at the underground cable side, because I figure robots will struggle in tight vaults longer. But that's still the same company, same union, I'm not jumping to something new. I'm not that guy.

S3.say: Five years is enough time for the union and the government to set rules, so let's not waste it. I'd even stand up and speak at a union meeting, which I've never done.
S3.think: Five years means I'd get my card and work qualified for a few years first. But I'd still be the junior guy near the bottom of the list when they pick who stays.
S3.do: Finishes his apprenticeship quickly and takes every overtime shift to push savings towards six months. Joins the union safety committee to have a say on robots near live lines.
S3.feel: Anxious, a slower and longer squeeze than the two-year picture.
S3.quote: I'd want them to remember the robot doesn't get electrocuted, but the guy standing next to it does.
S3.fieldNote: With more time his instinct is still collective rather than personal: committee work, speeches, safety rules. The only personal shift he'd consider is moving to underground work within the same company. Safety near live lines is the lever he thinks workers actually hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and if the government wastes it, that's on them. I'd tell people this is the time to fight for a shorter work week or some kind of payout for workers, while there's still time. I'd say it at the bar, at family dinners, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years almost feels worse in a weird way. It's like watching a truck come at you in slow motion. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have maybe seven years as a journeyman, and then what?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the normal plan: finish the apprenticeship, get my card, build savings to six months and keep it there. I'd stay deep in the union and campaign for a law on retraining money and wage guarantees. I'd probably wait a few years before making any big personal move, to see if it's really coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, just slower. A low hum instead of an alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd wait a few years. What would you be waiting to see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the robots can actually do a storm job. Like when a tree comes down on a line in the dark, on a hill, in the mud. If I see a robot do that, I'll believe it, and then I'll panic properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the ten years change your plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about maybe buying a small place. With ten years warning I'd want to buy sooner while I have steady pay, but Lena would say that's backwards, don't take a mortgage into a storm. I don't know who's right there.

S4.say: Ten years is fair warning, and if the government wastes it, that's on them. Now's the time to fight for a shorter work week or some kind of payout for workers.
S4.think: The slow version feels like watching a truck come at me in slow motion. I'd be thirty-seven with a few years as a journeyman, and then I don't know what.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and holds savings at about six months. Campaigns through the union for retraining money and wage guarantees, and waits a few years before any big personal move.
S4.feel: Still anxious, a low hum rather than an alarm.
S4.quote: If I see a robot do that, I'll believe it, and then I'll panic properly.
S4.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't calm him much, because he doesn't plan to change himself and the end point is the same. His test for belief is very concrete: a robot handling a storm job in mud and darkness. He and his partner disagree on whether to buy a home before it hits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy, because I wouldn't even be qualified yet. What would help is a law that says these companies can't just drop crews, and money to keep people paid while they figure out the next thing. I don't need a pep talk about learning to code. I need a paycheck that doesn't vanish.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's going to own the robots. If the public power company owns them and the savings come back to us, okay, I could live with that. If it's some private outfit renting them to the city, that's a different story.

headlineQuote: I don't need a pep talk about learning to code. I need a paycheck that doesn't vanish.
portrait: Adam is a 27-year-old third-year apprentice on a city distribution crew, who came to the trade late after four years in a warehouse and still feels behind. He doesn't use AI tools and doesn't want to, and he openly doubts he could learn to run robots. He trusts the union and the law far more than any personal plan. He stays calm if AI fizzles, uneasy about crew cuts in the steady picture, and alarmed by the two-year version because he'd never finish his apprenticeship. More warning time softens the blow only slightly, since his answer each time is to save, organise and wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would still be an unqualified apprentice when robots reached the lines.
whatWouldHelp: A law stopping companies from simply dropping crews, plus money to keep workers paid while they work out what comes next.
